summary: An overview of the Common Authentication Technology work, which aimed to give applications a common way to use authentication and related security services. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo describes an effort to separate applications' use of security services from the details of each security mechanism. A shared interface lets protocol callers request authentication without depending on one specific mechanism.

sections.title: Separating Security from Protocol Logic
sections.content:
The IETF's Common Authentication Technology (CAT) working group pursued related service interfaces and protocols. Its goal was to separate security implementation from integrating security data into caller protocols.

This separation lets one security implementation serve multiple protocols. Protocol implementers can focus on their protocol's functions rather than the details of individual security mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: A protocol should be able to request security services through a shared interface. It should not need to implement every security method itself.

sections.title: The GSS-API and Security Tokens
sections.content:
The working group developed the Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API), a mechanism-independent interface for callers. It provides peer-entity authentication and, with some underlying mechanisms, can provide data-origin authentication, integrity, and confidentiality.

The group also worked toward a common security-token format that identifies the mechanism used to interpret security data. RFC 1508 describes the GSS-API, and RFC 1509 specifies C-language bindings.
sections.plainLanguage: GSS-API gives protocols one interface for requesting authentication and related protection. The interface hides the details of the underlying security mechanism.

sections.title: Underlying Security Mechanisms
sections.content:
The CAT working group also considered technologies that implement the GSS-API model. The memo names Kerberos Version 5, based on secret-key cryptography, and Distributed Authentication Services, based on X.509 public-key technology.

The RFC presents these as candidate mechanisms documented in RFC 1510 and RFC 1507. It anticipates development of additional mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: Different security technologies can sit behind the same interface. The memo describes Kerberos V5 and Distributed Authentication Services as examples.
